newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--US durable goods orders bounced in April.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--US durable goods orders bounced in April.

text.p: U.S. durable goods orders rose in April in a partial bounceback from weak March orders, economists said.

In a Reuters poll, economists estimated, on average, that orders for durable goods rose 1.3 percent in April after dropping 2.6 percent in March. The April durable goods data are due on Wednesday, May 28 at 0915 EDT/1315 GMT.
"Orders for defense goods and commercial aircraft are likely to rebound," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "We see upside potential there."

Moran, who forecasted a 1.0 percent rise in April durable goods in total, said he also expected orders for electrical machinery and for industrial machinery to rebound in April after falling in March.
Automobile industry strikes in April probably depressed durable goods orders in that sector, economists said.
"We are looking for a drag from the auto sector," said Moran. "Vehicle assemblies dropped in April and that's why we're forecasting weaker orders, too," he said.
James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc, said durable goods orders would be up 1.0 percent excluding transportation.
"Non-defense capital goods excluding aircraft should rebound after falling 1.9 percent in March," said Glassman.
Non-defense capital goods orders including aircraft were down 4.0 percent in March.
A more decisive orders bounceback could become visible in the May data, reflecting the settlement of the auto industry labor disputes, economists said.
"New jobless claims fell off for most of May so the claims data are telling you that most of the strike problems are probably over," said Glassman.
In contrast, weekly jobless claims rose into the 340,000 to 350,000 area during April from 311,000 near the beginning of the month, he said.
Glassman said the April durable goods data was unlikely to change people's minds about the economy.
"We know April was soft for consumers and we're trying to figure out whether there's a slowing trend underway or just a pause," he said.
"The March and April data looked soggy across the board but they followed a couple of months of robust numbers," said Josh Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust.
Feinman said he expects "some snapback" from an orders decline in March but that due to auto strikes in April, he did not foresee "a full recouping" of March's losses.
Despite the subdued orders picture, Feinman said the economy has "a lot of strength" and is not slowing down enough on an underlying basis to forestall the risk of inflation.
